title: lock and await
sub: Why lock doesn't survive await, and how SemaphoreSlim works
cards/0/body:
The compiler won't allow it: error CS1996. To see why, look at what lock turns into. The compiler expands lock (x) { … } into (simplified) Monitor.Enter(x) and Monitor.Exit(x) in a finally. Monitor remembers the owner thread, and Exit from any other thread throws SynchronizationLockException.

If you get around the rule and call Monitor by hand, the code compiles and breaks:

  • console and server (no context): the continuation after await runs on a pool thread, not the one that took the lock. Its Monitor.Exit throws SynchronizationLockException, and the lock stays with the first thread. Any other thread that comes to this lock will wait forever;
  • WPF and WinForms (there is a context): the continuation comes back to the same UI thread, and Exit succeeds. But while the await is pending, the UI thread processes its queue, and a second click walks into the "taken" lock. Monitor is reentrant: the owner thread enters again without waiting. The lock protects nothing.
cards/0/deep: The exact expansion is Monitor.Enter(x, ref lockTaken) inside the try and if (lockTaken) Monitor.Exit(x) in the finally. Since C# 13 and .NET 9, lock on an object of type System.Threading.Lock expands into Lock.EnterScope(), but the rule is the same: the lock belongs to a thread, and CS1996 still applies.
cards/1/q: Why can't you await inside a lock?
cards/1/options/0: The lock belongs to a thread, and after await the method may continue on another thread
cards/1/options/1: await inside a lock is too slow
cards/1/options/2: lock can't work with Task objects
cards/1/explain: lock is Monitor.Enter and Monitor.Exit, and only the owner thread can release a Monitor. After await the continuation may run on another pool thread, and Exit from there throws SynchronizationLockException.
cards/2/q: A console app's async Main gets around CS1996 and calls Monitor by hand. What happens at Monitor.Exit?
cards/2/options/0: SynchronizationLockException: Exit is called by a pool thread that never took the lock
cards/2/options/1: Nothing: a Monitor can be released from any thread
cards/2/options/2: Deadlock: Exit waits until the owner thread releases the lock
cards/2/explain: The main thread called Enter. A console app has no context, so the continuation after Task.Delay runs on a pool thread. Monitor checks the owner and throws, and the lock stays with the main thread.
cards/2/wrong/1: Monitor remembers its owner thread and can be released only by it.
cards/2/wrong/2: Exit doesn't wait for anything: it checks the owner and throws right away.
cards/3/q: WPF: the same hand-written Monitor around an await in a click handler. While the first SaveAsync waits for the database, the user clicks again. What happens?
cards/3/options/0: The second handler gets in: the UI thread already owns the lock, and Monitor is reentrant
cards/3/options/1: The second click waits until the first handler leaves the lock
cards/3/explain: One UI thread runs both handlers. While the first one sits at its await, the thread processes the queue and runs the second handler. Monitor sees the owner and just bumps its entry count. Two saves run at the same time, even though the lock is "taken".
cards/3/wrong/1: The owner enters without waiting. And if Enter did wait, it would block the UI thread, which still has to run the first handler's continuation.
cards/3/wrong/2: An owner entering again isn't an error: Monitor is reentrant.
cards/4/body:
SemaphoreSlim has no owner, only a count of free slots. The constructor SemaphoreSlim(initialCount, maxCount) takes how many slots are free now and how many there can be at most. (1, 1) is an async lock for one; (3, 3) lets up to three in at once.

  • WaitAsync(): if the count is above zero, it decrements it and returns an already completed task. The await takes the fast path, with no pause (section 3).
  • If the count is zero, it puts you in the queue of waiters and returns an unfinished task. The method stops at the await, and the thread is free.
  • Release(): if someone is waiting, it completes the task of one of the waiters, and the slot passes to them. Which one isn't guaranteed: no order, not even FIFO, is promised. If nobody is waiting, it increments the count. Releasing beyond maxCount throws SemaphoreFullException.

There's no owner, so you can release from any thread, after await too. WaitAsync has an overload with a token: WaitAsync(ct). If it's canceled, it throws OperationCanceledException, and you didn't get a slot. That's why WaitAsync goes before the try: the Release in finally must give back only the slot you took.
cards/5/explain: The semaphore has Wait() too, but it blocks the thread until a slot is free. Enter is a Monitor method; SemaphoreSlim doesn't have it.
cards/6/options/0: 3 free slots out of 3: up to three get in at once
cards/6/options/1: One can be inside, and three more wait in the queue
cards/6/options/2: Three attempts to get in, then an exception
cards/6/explain: The first number is how many slots are free now, the second is the maximum. Each WaitAsync takes a slot, each Release gives one back. This is how you limit concurrency, for example the number of simultaneous requests to an API.
cards/7/q: SemaphoreSlim(3, 3), all three slots are taken. What happens on a fourth await _gate.WaitAsync()?
cards/7/options/0: WaitAsync returns an unfinished task: the method stops at the await, and the thread is free until someone calls Release
cards/7/options/1: The thread blocks until someone calls Release
cards/7/options/2: WaitAsync throws: there are no slots
cards/7/explain: The count is zero, so the caller joins the queue of waiters. Release will hand the slot to it: it completes its task, and the method continues after the await.
cards/8/body:
Monitor's owner gets in the way of async code. SemaphoreSlim has no owner, and that has a price too: the semaphore doesn't know that "it's you again". Entering the same semaphore again from the same call chain is a silent deadlock. No exception, the task just never completes.

  • 1. SaveAsync takes the only slot; the count is 0.
  • 2. Inside, SaveAsync awaits FlushAsync, which also calls WaitAsync on _gate. There's no slot, so FlushAsync joins the queue.
  • 3. Only the Release in SaveAsync's finally gives the slot back. But SaveAsync is waiting for FlushAsync. Each waits for the other.

The fix is not to take the lock twice. The inner method works without the lock (it's often called …Core), and only the outer one takes it.
cards/9/q: _gate = new SemaphoreSlim(1, 1). What happens when RefreshAsync is called?
cards/9/options/0: RefreshAsync hangs forever: GetAsync waits for a slot that only RefreshAsync itself will give back
cards/9/options/1: It works: the same call chain is already inside, as with Monitor
cards/9/explain: The semaphore has no owner, so it doesn't know GetAsync was called from inside the lock. The count is 0, GetAsync joins the queue, and RefreshAsync waits for GetAsync. Nobody ever reaches Release.
cards/9/wrong/1: That's Monitor's reentrancy. SemaphoreSlim counts slots, not threads or calls.
cards/9/wrong/2: SemaphoreFullException comes from an extra Release, and here nobody reaches Release at all.
cards/10/q: Why does WaitAsync(ct) go before the try rather than as the first line inside it?
cards/10/options/0: If the wait is canceled, finally releases a slot you never took, and an extra caller gets in
cards/10/options/1: Inside a try, WaitAsync blocks the thread
cards/10/options/2: Inside a try it doesn't compile
cards/10/explain: On cancellation WaitAsync(ct) throws OperationCanceledException, and no slot was taken. But finally still calls Release: a slot frees up while its owner is still inside, and someone else gets in. Later an extra Release hits the maximum and throws SemaphoreFullException.
cards/11/q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
cards/11/options/0: WaitAsync doesn't block the thread while it waits for a slot
cards/11/options/1: SemaphoreSlim can be released from a different thread
cards/11/options/2: A second WaitAsync from the same call chain gets in, like re-entering a Monitor
cards/11/options/3: Monitor.Exit can be called from any thread
cards/11/options/4: You can skip Release: the GC will give the slot back
cards/11/explain: The semaphore has no owner: you can release it from anywhere, but it also won't recognize "your" repeated entry. Monitor, on the contrary, remembers its owner and can be released only by it. Nobody will give a semaphore slot back for you.
cards/12/pairs/0/1: Monitor: the lock belongs to a thread
cards/12/pairs/3/1: Wait for a slot without blocking the thread
